label: L2
title: Context Engineering: Knowledge and Instructions
brief: An LLM outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Decoding chooses from it either greedily or by sampling, and temperature sharpens (T < 1) or flattens (T > 1) the distribution before sampling. Models cannot know facts newer than their training data, so retrieval-augmented generation selects relevant content (web search or a proprietary index scored with BM25), packs it into the prompt, and sends it to the LLM. Instructions work only because of post-training: pre-training is next-word prediction, which produces a text continuer, while supervised fine-tuning on about 12,500 human-written answers plus RLHF (a reward model trained on human rankings, then PPO) produces an instruction follower. The same post-training recipe explains output contracts: free-text answers parsed with regexes break when the model changes, whereas schema forcing yields 100% parseable output because models were trained to fill in a schema that appears in their context. Few-shot examples matter less today but still help when the model cannot know a proprietary label set or process.
kp: Greedy decoding takes the top token (not necessarily optimal; beam search can help); random sampling draws in proportion to probability.
Temperature reshapes the distribution: T = 0.5 sharpens (stormy 0.80), T = 5 flattens, T = 50 is nearly uniform.
Sampling a low-probability token early can derail the rest of the generated response.
RAG = (1) select relevant content, (2) pack it into the prompt, (3) send it to the LLM; sources are a search API or your own index (chunks scored by BM25, top k).
Pre-training is causal language modeling (next-word prediction); GPT-3 has 96 layers and 96 heads and trained on about 500B tokens, mostly Common Crawl.
Base models continue text rather than follow instructions (GPT-3 and Qwen 2.5 Base examples).
Post-training = SFT (about 12,500 human-written pairs) + RLHF (rankings on 33,000 instructions train a reward model; PPO on about 31,000 questions).
Terminology: base model = pre-training only; instruction-tuned = pre-training + SFT; post-training = SFT + RLHF.
Output contracts: regex parsing is fragile across models (gpt-4o found a team in 1/100 answers); schema forcing parsed 100/100 with 69-74% accuracy.
Prompt anatomy: instructions, knowledge, and optionally examples; few-shot still helps for proprietary codes or processes.

topics.x: At each step the model gives a probability for every possible next token. Greedy decoding takes the most likely token; random sampling draws in proportion to probability, which can occasionally pick a low-probability token and derail the response. Temperature reshapes the distribution before sampling: low T concentrates mass on the head, high T makes the tail real, and very high T is close to uniform.

A model cannot know facts newer than its training data (it confidently mislabels Moo Deng, a pygmy hippo who went viral in September 2024). Retrieval-augmented generation selects relevant content, packs it into the prompt, and sends it to the LLM, asking it to answer only from those sources with citations. Content comes from a public search API or from your own index: chunk documents, score chunks (e.g., BM25), keep the top k.

Pre-training is next-word prediction on huge text collections (causal language modeling): every prefix of a sentence is an input and its next word the label. GPT-3 (96 layers, 96 heads) trained on Common Crawl 410B, Books2 55B, WebText2 19B, Books1 12B and Wikipedia 3B tokens. A base model continues text, so a request often gets more questions or rambling back, because it was never trained to answer instructions.

Step 1 (SFT): humans wrote about 12,500 high-quality instruction-answer pairs, and GPT-3 was trained further on them by next-word prediction. Steps 2-3 (RLHF): for 33,000 instructions GPT-3 sampled several answers that humans ranked; pairs (instruction, preferred, other) trained a reward model that scores any (instruction, answer); its ratings then nudged GPT-3's weights with PPO on about 31,000 questions. That is how GPT-3 became GPT-3.5/InstructGPT, and the recipe is largely unchanged today.

Downstream code needs machine-readable answers. Parsing free text (e.g., a regex for bolded team names) found a team in 178/200 cases with 64% accuracy, and broke when the model changed (gpt-4o: 1/100). Passing a JSON schema via response_format gave 100/100 parseable outputs and 69-74% accuracy. The model still sees one flat token sequence; it complies because post-training on (instruction + schema, conforming answer) pairs taught it to fill in the shape it sees.

A prompt is roughly instructions plus knowledge plus optional examples. Few-shot prompting (e.g., Good English/Poor English pairs, after which GPT-3 fixes grammar) matters less now that post-trained models follow plain instructions. Examples still help when the model cannot know something, such as proprietary department codes for routing or a specific internal process.

cards.b: Greedy: always pick the highest-probability next token. Random sampling: draw a token in proportion to its probability.
cards.x: Greedy is not necessarily optimal; beam search can help.

cards.f: What can go wrong with random sampling?
cards.b: A low-probability token can happen to be chosen, and the rest of the response builds on it and goes off track.
cards.x: Every later token is conditioned on the earlier choices.

cards.f: Effect of temperature on the next-token distribution?
cards.b: T < 1 sharpens it (head takes almost everything); T > 1 flattens it; very large T is almost uniform. Over 4 tokens, stormy goes 0.80 (T = 0.5), 0.44 (T = 5), 0.27 (T = 50).
cards.x: 'aardvark' rises from 3 in 10,000 (T = 1) to 1 in 10 (T = 5) to 1 in 4 (T = 50).

cards.f: Why do we need RAG? (Moo Deng example)
cards.b: The needed knowledge is public but newer than the model: asked about Moo Deng, it invents a social-media influencer, but Moo Deng is a pygmy hippo born July 2024.
cards.x: Fluent and confident does not mean correct.

cards.b: (1) Select relevant content (search API or your index), (2) pack it into the prompt, (3) send it to the LLM, e.g., 'Answer using only the sources below. Cite them as [1], [2].'
cards.x: The model is unchanged; only its context changes.

cards.f: RAG over a proprietary database: how is content selected?
cards.b: Split your documents into chunks, score each chunk against the query (token counts, BM25), keep the top k, and pack them with the question.
cards.x: Use when the knowledge is private, not just recent.

cards.b: Next-word prediction on vast text: each prefix of a sentence is an input and the following word is its 'fake' label.
cards.x: This yields something that continues text, not something that follows instructions.

cards.b: 96 Transformer layers, 96 heads per attention layer. Tokens: Common Crawl 410B, Books2 55B, WebText2 19B, Books1 12B, Wikipedia 3B (about 500B total).
cards.x: Common Crawl is about 82% of the tokens.

cards.f: Why do pre-trained (base) models give unhelpful answers?
cards.b: They were never explicitly trained to answer instructions; they just keep generating the next word based on patterns from their training text.
cards.x: Qwen 2.5 Base answers a routing question with more questions; Qwen 2.5 Instruct answers it.

cards.b: Humans wrote about 12,500 high-quality instruction-answer pairs; GPT-3 was trained further on them with next-word prediction.
cards.x: It works, but writing good answers is slow and expensive.

cards.f: How is the reward model built?
cards.b: 33,000 instructions; GPT-3 samples several answers to each; humans rank them; each data point is [instruction, preferred answer A, other answer B]; train a model to rate any (instruction, answer).
cards.x: Ranking someone else's answers is much easier than writing one.

cards.f: How does the reward model improve GPT-3?
cards.b: Generate an answer, have the reward model rate it (e.g., 1.5 for bad, 3.2 for good), and use the rating to nudge GPT-3's weights with PPO, repeated on about 31,000 questions.

cards.f: Lecture terminology: pre-training, post-training, base model, instruction-tuned model?
cards.b: Pre-training = next-word prediction on vast text. Post-training = SFT + RLHF. Base model = pre-training only. Instruction-tuned model = pre-training + SFT.
cards.x: In this terminology, instruction-tuned does not require RLHF.

cards.f: Why is regex-parsing model output fragile?
cards.b: A change of model changes the answer style, which changes the pattern you must look for. The bold-text parser found a team in 178/200 answers (64% accuracy) but only 1/100 for gpt-4o.
cards.x: The failure is in the contract, not in the model's routing ability.

cards.f: What is schema forcing, and what did it achieve?
cards.b: Passing response_format = {type: json_schema, json_schema: SCHEMA}. It parsed 100/100 for gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-4o, with 70%, 69% and 74% accuracy.
cards.x: This kind of output contract is a core ingredient for agents.

cards.f: Why does an LLM stick to a JSON schema it only sees as flat text?
cards.b: Post-training on (instruction + schema, conforming answer) pairs by next-word prediction teaches that when that shape is in the context, the well-scoring continuation fills it in.
cards.x: It is SFT step 1 again with a different answer column.

o: Always choosing the highest-probability next token
Sampling a token in proportion to its probability
Sampling uniformly among all tokens
Keeping several candidate sequences and picking the best
quiz.e: Greedy takes the argmax at every step. Keeping several candidate sequences is beam search, which the slide mentions as a possible improvement.

quiz.q: About how many human-written instruction-answer pairs were used for supervised fine-tuning of GPT-3?
o: About 12,500
About 33,000
About 31,000
About 410 billion
quiz.e: SFT used about 12,500 human-written pairs. 33,000 is the number of instructions whose sampled answers humans ranked for the reward model; 31,000 is the RL step.

quiz.q: In the lecture's terminology, an 'instruction-tuned' model is built with:
o: Pre-training + supervised fine-tuning
Pre-training only
Pre-training + RAG
RLHF alone, without pre-training
quiz.e: Base model = pre-training only; instruction-tuned = pre-training + SFT; post-training as a whole = SFT + RLHF. RAG changes the prompt, not the model.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of RAG?
o: Select relevant content, pack it into the prompt, send it to the LLM
Fine-tune, evaluate, deploy
Tokenize, embed, decode
Sample, rank, reward
quiz.e: RAG leaves the model's weights unchanged and changes only its context. Sample, rank and reward describes RLHF data collection.

quiz.q: Which source supplied the most GPT-3 training tokens?
o: Common Crawl (filtered), 410B
Books2, 55B
WebText2, 19B
Wikipedia, 3B
quiz.e: Common Crawl is 410B of about 499B tokens (about 82%). Wikipedia is the smallest at 3B.

quiz.q: Renormalized over two tokens, stormy has 0.6 and rainy 0.3 at T = 1 (probabilities scale as $p^{1/T}$). What is P(stormy) at T = 0.5?
quiz.e: $0.6^2=0.36$, $0.3^2=0.09$, so $0.36/0.45=0.80$, matching the slide. 0.67 is the T = 1 renormalized value, $0.6/0.9$.

quiz.q: What happens to the next-token distribution when temperature goes from 1 to 50?
o: It becomes almost uniform; nonsense tokens like 'aardvark' rise to about 1 in 4
It sharpens so the head takes almost everything
Nothing; temperature affects only greedy decoding
Low-probability tokens are removed
quiz.e: High T flattens the distribution: at T = 50 the four tokens get 0.27, 0.27, 0.23, 0.23. Sharpening is what T < 1 does.

quiz.q: Why does RLHF collect human rankings of sampled answers instead of more human-written answers?
o: Ranking answers someone else wrote is much easier and cheaper than writing high-quality answers
Rankings are more precise labels than written answers
Human-written answers cannot be used for training
Ranking needs no human input
quiz.e: SFT helped, but writing high-quality answers to thousands of instructions is difficult and expensive. Rankings still need humans; they are just cheaper to produce.

quiz.q: What does a single reward-model training data point look like?
o: [instruction, preferred answer A, other answer B]
[instruction, human-written answer]
[instruction, numeric score from 1 to 5]
[prefix, next word]
quiz.e: Humans rank answers, and each ranked pair becomes (instruction, preferred, other). [instruction, human answer] is SFT data; [prefix, next word] is pre-training.

quiz.q: Which algorithm uses the reward model's ratings to update GPT-3's weights?
o: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
BM25
Beam search
Supervised next-word prediction on the ratings
quiz.e: The rating 'nudges' the weights through PPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm. BM25 scores retrieval chunks in RAG, and beam search is a decoding method.

quiz.q: With the bold-text parser, gpt-4o found a team in 1/100 answers (0% accuracy), but with schema forcing it reached 74%. What best explains the gap?
o: gpt-4o's answer style broke the regex, so parsing failed rather than routing
gpt-4o is worse at routing complaints than the mini models
Schema forcing hands the model the correct labels
gpt-4o refuses to answer routing questions
quiz.e: Changing models changes answer style, which breaks the parsing pattern. Under schema forcing gpt-4o is actually the most accurate (74%), so its routing ability was never the problem.

quiz.q: How does the model actually receive a JSON schema passed through response_format?
o: As part of one flat token sequence in the prompt; it still emits one token at a time
As a structured object it can query while generating
As a grammar it is retrained on for each request
It never sees the schema; the API rewrites the free-text answer afterwards
quiz.e: The API serializes the user message and schema into one string; the model never sees a list, dict or schema object. That is why it needs post-training to respect the schema.

quiz.q: When are few-shot examples still worth including in a prompt today?
o: When routing to internal department codes the model cannot know
When correcting English grammar
When summarizing a news article
When translating common phrases
quiz.e: Post-trained models handle generic tasks like 'correct the grammar' from instructions alone. Examples still help when the model has no way to know the labels or a proprietary process.

quiz.q: With probabilities proportional to $p^{1/T}$, stormy (0.6) and rainy (0.3) have a 2:1 ratio at T = 1. What is P(stormy)/P(rainy) at T = 5?
o: 2 (unchanged)
$\sqrt{2}\approx1.41$
quiz.e: $(0.6/0.3)^{1/5}=2^{0.2}\approx1.15$, consistent with the slide's 0.442/0.385. $2^5$ is what T = 1/5 (sharpening) would give.

quiz.q: According to the lecture, why does an LLM keep to a JSON schema it sees only as flat text?
o: Post-training on (instruction + schema, conforming answer) pairs taught it that the well-scoring continuation fills in that shape
It parses the JSON into a dictionary internally
The temperature is set to 0 whenever a schema is given
RAG retrieves the schema's documentation
quiz.e: It is SFT step 1 again with a different answer column: the schema is part of the input and the training target is a conforming JSON answer. Temperature and retrieval have nothing to do with it.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the GPT-3 to InstructGPT recipe?
o: SFT on human-written pairs, then humans rank sampled answers, then train a reward model, then RL (PPO) with its ratings
Train the reward model, then SFT, then PPO
PPO, then SFT, then train the reward model
Humans rank answers, then PPO, then SFT, then train the reward model
quiz.e: The reward model must exist before PPO can use its ratings, and SFT comes first on human-written answers. Steps 2-3 together are RLHF.

quiz.q: Your bank wants an LLM to route complaints to internal team codes and feed the result directly into code. Which design follows the lecture?
o: List the internal codes (with a few examples) in the prompt and enforce a JSON schema whose team field is an enum of those codes
Use a base model and parse bolded text from its answer
Raise the temperature so the model explores more codes
Run RAG over the public web to find the codes
quiz.e: Internal codes are knowledge the model cannot have, so they go in the prompt (examples help here), and a schema enum gives a parseable output contract. Base models do not follow instructions, and regex parsing is fragile.

written.q: Explain how a pre-trained base model such as GPT-3 becomes an instruction-following model like InstructGPT. Cover what pre-training optimizes and why that falls short, each post-training step with its data, what the reward model learns, and the difference between a base model and an instruction-tuned model.
written.m: Pre-training is causal language modeling: next-word prediction on vast text (GPT-3: 96 layers, about 500B tokens, mostly Common Crawl). The result continues text and was never trained to answer instructions, so requests get rambling continuations (GPT-3, Qwen 2.5 Base). Step 1, SFT: humans write about 12,500 high-quality instruction-answer pairs, and the model is trained further on them with next-word prediction; this helps but is expensive to scale. Step 2: for 33,000 instructions the model samples several answers and humans rank them (easier than writing); ranked pairs [instruction, preferred, other] train a reward model that rates any (instruction, answer), in effect learning how humans rank responses. Step 3: the model's answers are scored by the reward model and its weights nudged with PPO on about 31,000 questions. Steps 2-3 are RLHF; post-training = SFT + RLHF. A base model has pre-training only; an instruction-tuned model has pre-training + SFT.
k: Pre-training = next-word prediction; base models just continue text
SFT with about 12,500 human-written pairs, trained by next-word prediction
Ranking 33,000 instructions' answers; pairwise data; reward model learns human preferences
PPO using reward ratings (about 31,000 questions); steps 2-3 = RLHF
Correct terminology: base vs instruction-tuned vs post-training

written.q: Design a reliable LLM component that routes consumer-finance complaints to one of your firm's internal teams and returns output another program consumes. Address knowledge, instructions and output format, decoding, and examples, and justify each choice with evidence from the lecture.
written.m: Knowledge: the model cannot know your internal team list or recent policies, so put the team codes and any needed policy text in the prompt, retrieved from your own index when large (chunk, score with BM25, pack the top k), as in RAG. Instructions: use a post-trained (instruction-tuned) model; base models continue text rather than follow instructions. Output contract: do not regex-parse free text. The bold-parser found a team in only 178/200 answers (64% accuracy), and switching to gpt-4o collapsed it to 1/100. Enforce response_format with a JSON schema, e.g. {reasoning: string, team: enum of codes}; schema forcing parsed 100/100 across three models with 69-74% accuracy. It works because post-training on (instruction + schema, conforming answer) pairs taught models to fill in the shape. Decoding: sampling can pick low-probability tokens and derail answers, and high temperature flattens the distribution toward nonsense, so use low temperature or greedy decoding for a classification task. Examples: few-shot is unnecessary for generic tasks but worthwhile here because the model cannot know your department codes.
k: Codes and policy knowledge supplied in context (RAG or prompt), with reason
Use an instruction-tuned model; base models don't follow instructions
Schema forcing with an enum, citing parse and accuracy numbers vs regex
Low temperature or greedy, tied to sampling risk
